findings.title: Bytecode tick example cannot advance ordinary rooms
findings.description: The session example claims its tick advances room state, but its hook always writes the fixed path rooms/system and sets tick to the literal string "1". The owning runtime confines tick-hook mutations to the current room subtree, so a tick for rooms/<roomId> discards the rooms/system mutation unless the room itself is named system. In addition, DocumentPlugin.updateField overwrites a field and cannot increment it. Consequently the advertised server-authoritative loop is a no-op for ordinary rooms and never advances a counter even in the system room.
findings.recommendation: Do not present updateField as an advancing game tick. Use session.live for counters and simulation logic, or show a bytecode tick that performs a supported status transition within the current room's scope. Ensure the example's prose and full worked policy use the corrected pattern.

findings.title: Intent writes are not bound to room membership
findings.description: The intent create rule proves only that the caller uses their own playerId and player field. It never verifies that the caller is a member of the attacker-selected roomId. There is no player membership document in the example. Any authenticated outsider can therefore append valid, rate-capped intents beneath any known room. A tick that consumes the documented intent subtree can process those outsider inputs, allowing unauthorized participation, griefing, or influence over settled results. The per-user rolling cap limits frequency but does not establish room authorization.
findings.recommendation: Declare a trusted room-membership record and require it in the intent create rule, such as a get() check against a server- or owner-created member row for roomId and user.id. Keep the playerId and payload identity bindings as additional checks.
